Sourced facts already located: (a) Castryck-Laterveer-Ounaies 2012, Definition 1 (research/sources/castryck2012_degree12_html.full.md line 129): 'f_H^{(j)} denotes the j-th Hasse derivative... it makes no difference in characteristic 0 or p > d−1'; the bad-prime lists p=2 (d=3) and {3,5,7} (d=4) are stated immediately after (line ~136). (b) Schaub-Spivakovsky 2023 (research/sources/schaub_spivakovsky_bad-primes_2023.full.md lines 50-53): H_i(f)=sum_j C(j,i)..., 'i-th Hasse derivative', CA defined via gcd(f, H_i(f)). (c) Ghosh 2025 (research/sources/ghosh2025_proof_html.full.md lines 37-43): f_i = Hasse-Schmidt derivative, f_i = f^{(i)}/i! in char 0. Decision: published char-p bad-prime lists use HASSE derivatives. Ordinary i-th derivative = i!·H_i, so the conventions agree in char 0 and p≥n; in char p<n the ordinary derivative can vanish identically (vacuity). Write a claim (id hasse-vs-ordinary-definitions) with these anchors and holds-here, and see research/threads/hasse-vs-ordinary.md.

fields.detail: n=5 bad-prime verification via the Schaub-Spivakovsky minors criterion, switched from SNF to rank over F_p. RESULT (measured, not asserted): the SNF route is feasible at n=4 (19x15 matrices, all 64 tuples, milliseconds, lcm J_T=1575 -> {3,5,7}) and infeasible at n=5 (195x120 matrices, 4^4=256 tuples; a single SNF did not finish within a 90s cap - code/out/commands.log final command 'SNF exceeded 90s cap on one 195x120 matrix'). Projected lower bound 256*90s = 6.4h, and the SNF cost is super-polynomial, so the full route is out of budget by orders of magnitude. Do NOT re-run SNF at n=5 with a longer alarm. Instead: p is bad for n=5 iff rank_{F_p}(M_T) < 120 for some T in {1..5}^4 (C=120 columns; lib.badprimes.rank_mod_p is modular Gaussian elimination, O(D*C^2) per tuple). Deciding a NAMED prime needs only the rank drop, never J_T itself, so test the candidate primes directly: the literature's degree-5 bad list {2,3,7,11,131,193,599,3541,8009} (Castryck 2012 Thm 4, lines ~147-149; Chellali-Salinier HAL hal-00748843). Report which primes are bad for n=5 and compare against that list. Capture to code/out/badprimes_n5.captured.txt with a header naming the program, the oracle function (rank_mod_p), the base ring (Z matrix, rank over F_p), the term order (not used: exact matrix rank), the worker count, and the search space (256 tuples x the prime list).

Deciding a NAMED prime needs only the rank drop, never J_T itself, so test the candidate primes directly: the literature's degree-5 bad list {2,3,7,11,131,193,599,3541,8009} (Castryck 2012 Thm 4, lines ~147-149; Chellali-Salinier HAL hal-00748843). Report which primes are bad for n=5 and compare against that list. fields.detail: The n=20 certified-bad frontier (claim badprimes-n20-certified-frontier) rests entirely on the sufficient binomial criterion p | C(n,i)-1 (Schaub-Spivakovsky 2023, arXiv:2307.05997 Cor 8). Quantify this under-capture at the degrees where the true bad list is known (n=3 {2}, n=4 {3,5,7}, n=5 {2,3,7,11,131,193,599,3541,8009}) and confirm it never falsely condemns a known good prime on the small primes. fields.reason: Binomial bad-prime criterion calibrated against true lists at the degrees where the full list is known. Exact integer arithmetic (lib.badprimes.criterion_bad_primes, sympy factorint; primary source Schaub-Spivakovsky 2023 arXiv:2307.05997 Cor 8). True lists sourced from Castryck-Laterveer-Ounaies 2012 Thm 4 / Sec 1.7. Results: n=3 certified {2} of {2} (ratio 1.0); n=4 certified {3,5} of {3,5,7} (gap {7}, ratio 2/3); n=5 certified {2,3} of the 9 true bad primes, missing {7,11,131,193,599,3541,8009} (ratio 2/9 = 22%). Negative control: first 10 good primes at each degree divide no C(n,i)-1 (30 checks, never falsely condemns). Takeaway: the binomial criterion is sufficient, never exhaustive; the n=20 frontier's 18 certified primes are a LOWER BOUND on the true degree-20 bad set and its 'candidate good' primes are not proven good (by analogy with n=5 catching 2 of 9). fields.detail: Directive 6 step (1) — first execution of an adopted approach. Verify, symbolically and exactly (sympy, oracle-guarded), the identity R_i = c_n · ∏_{β root of f} e_{n−i}(β−β_1,…,β−β_n), equivalently the Hasse–Taylor step H_i(f)(x) = e_{n−i}(x−β_1,…,x−β_n), over QQ for n = 4,5,6 AND over F_p for n = p+1 at p = 2,3,5, by expanding both sides in the roots and checking the resultant-factorization against lib.casas_alvero.
